clue.text: Heretic in steep fall in river

indicators.note: the second 'in' says the steep fall sits within the river's name

parts.note: the Wye is a river on the England-Wales border
a cliff is a sheer drop of rock

explanation.surface: A heretic tumbles down a precipice into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wye is a river on the border of England and Wales; CLIFF goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: John Wycliffe, the fourteenth-century reformer, was condemned by the Church for heresy.

clue.text: Sounds like a caprice of Sayers

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a creation of Dorothy L. Sayers

indicators.note: the clue openly says the word for a caprice is matched by its pronunciation

parts.note: a whimsy is a fanciful notion or caprice

explanation.surface: A remark that something fanciful resembles the novelist Dorothy Sayers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of Sayers' defines the detective belonging to Dorothy L. Sayers: Lord Peter, her aristocratic sleuth.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Peter, the aristocratic amateur detective, is the hero of Dorothy L. Sayers's novels.

clue.text: With as little a web as this will I ensnare as great a fly as "(Othello)

definitions.text: With as little a web as this will I ensnare as great a fly as "(Othello)

parts.words: With as little a web as this will I ensnare as great a fly as "(Othello)
parts.note: Iago's aside in Othello, with the name of the lieutenant he plans to trap left out for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A line of Iago's from Othello with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago watches the lieutenant take Desdemona's hand and says he will catch him in a web of small courtesies; the missing word is that lieutenant's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation's gap is filled by the name of Othello's lieutenant, the fly Iago means to ensnare.

clue.text: Producers of primaries, perhaps

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters of primaries are only one possible arrangement, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A question of who stages the primary elections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Producers of primaries' reads as election organisers; 'perhaps' asks for the letters of PRIMARIES rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Impresarios (Italian plural impresari) are theatrical or operatic producers who stage shows.

clue.text: Cowardly description of satanic types?

parts.note: 'Cowardly' means written by Noel Coward, whose comedy title also describes the rebel spirits cast out of heaven

explanation.surface: A taunt that devils are chickens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardly' looks like timid, but it means 'by Noel Coward', the English playwright whose 1925 comedy bears this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel Coward's play has this title, and Satan's followers expelled from heaven are the rebel angels who fell.

clue.text: Sylvia Townsend Warner's collection (of dishonest folk)

definitions.text: Sylvia Townsend Warner's collection (of dishonest folk)

parts.words: Sylvia Townsend Warner's collection (of dishonest folk)
parts.note: Sylvia Townsend Warner's book The ... of Cheats; the bracket hints at the rest of its title

explanation.surface: A novelist's gathering of rogues.
explanation.walkthrough: Sylvia Townsend Warner's 1947 story collection is called The Museum of Cheats; 'dishonest folk' are the cheats.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallery displaying a collection is a museum, and Warner's title displays a collection of cheats.

clue.text: Where Cato died in Rajput (I can hardly associate it with New York)

indicators.note: 'in' says the place lies inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A geography lesson confusing an Indian warrior, a Roman statesman and a New York town.
explanation.walkthrough: The town is tucked inside 'RajpUT I CAn'. The bracketed remark is comment: there is also a city of that name in New York State.
explanation.definitionFit: Cato the Younger killed himself at this North African city in 46 BC rather than submit to Caesar.

clue.text: "These strong — fetters I must break, / Or lose myself in dotage" (Antony and Cleopatra)

definitions.text: "These strong — fetters I must break, / Or lose myself in dotage" (Antony and Cleopatra)

parts.words: "These strong — fetters I must break, / Or lose myself in dotage" (Antony and Cleopatra)
parts.note: Antony's words about the hold Cleopatra's land and queen have on him, with the adjective missing

explanation.surface: Antony resolving to break free of Cleopatra.
explanation.walkthrough: Antony means the chains of his love for the Queen of the Nile; the gap is the adjective for her country.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra was queen of the Nile kingdom, so the fetters Antony must break are those of that land.

clue.text: One of Scott's legendary places

parts.note: Walter Scott's novel A Legend of ... is named for a place, so the place is 'legendary' in his title

explanation.surface: A tourist's note about romantic Scottish settings.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's novel A Legend of Montrose takes its title from the Marquis named after the Scottish town on the Angus coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's novel title names this Angus town, making it a place with a legend attached by him.

clue.text: Short review of The Young Visiters

definitions.text: Short review of The Young Visiters

parts.words: Short review of The Young Visiters
parts.note: a one-word verdict on Daisy Ashford's novel, written aged nine, whose title and text are full of childish spelling errors

explanation.surface: A brief critique of a famous children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Daisy Ashford wrote The Young Visiters at nine; 'Visiters' itself shows the faulty spelling that fills the book.
explanation.definitionFit: The book's charm lies in its wrongly written words, so a one-word review calls it incorrectly spelt.

clue.text: Age shall not weary him, nor the years condemn

definitions.text: Age shall not weary him, nor the years condemn

parts.words: Age shall not weary him, nor the years condemn
parts.note: the famous line from 'For the Fallen', with 'them' changed to 'him' to point to the poet himself

explanation.surface: A memorial tribute to a man who will never grow old.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from the 1914 poem 'For the Fallen' reads 'them'; the setter turns it on its author, Laurence Binyon.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Binyon wrote 'For the Fallen', the remembrance poem containing this line, so his reputation endures.

clue.text: Haydn's beak

parts.note: Haydn's Symphony No. 55 has a nickname that is also British slang 'beak', a teacher

explanation.surface: A composer's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beak' looks like a nose, but in British school slang a beak is a teacher; Haydn's Symphony No. 55 carries that nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: A beak is British slang for a teacher, the nickname given to Haydn's Symphony No. 55.

clue.text: English distance covered by 17

definitions.note: the subject treated in a book by the writer at 17-down

parts.note: a mile is a measure of distance

explanation.surface: An English distance run by a fellow competitor.
explanation.walkthrough: The author at 17-down wrote a treatise on education named after its pupil, the subject it covers.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1762 treatise on education by the author at 17-down is named after the boy it describes.

clue.text: Nabokov, then Crane, might produce this magician

indicators.note: 'might produce' says the letters of then Crane can be worked into something new

explanation.surface: Two writers in sequence conjuring up a wizard.
explanation.walkthrough: Nabokov wrote the novella The Enchanter; 'might produce' asks for the letters of THEN CRANE rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An enchanter is a sorcerer who casts spells, and Nabokov's novella bears this title.

clue.text: Welsh writer who wrote of American candy?

definitions.text: Welsh writer who wrote of American candy?

parts.words: Welsh writer who wrote of American candy?
parts.note: this Welsh author wrote the play Taffy, which is also the American name for a chewy sweet

explanation.surface: A Welsh author writing about sweets from the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: The Welsh author's play is called Taffy: British slang for a Welshman, but in America a chewy candy.
explanation.definitionFit: Caradoc Evans was the Welsh writer whose 1923 play, Taffy, shares its name with American toffee.

clue.text: Rewritten tensely, an ordinary Victorian novel

indicators.note: 'Rewritten' says the letters of tensely and an are written out again in a new order

explanation.surface: A commonplace nineteenth-century novel recast in a tense style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rewritten' rearranges the letters of TENSELY and AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen Wood's 1861 sensation novel was hugely popular, a commonplace of the Victorian lending library.

clue.text: Like some of Shaw's work, he felt

definitions.text: Like some of Shaw's work, he felt

parts.words: Like some of Shaw's work, he felt
parts.note: Shaw grouped his early plays into two volumes, one labelled agreeable and the other its opposite

explanation.surface: A remark about how Shaw rated his own plays.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw published Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant in 1898; the 'pleasant' ones were the volume he himself called so.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's own label for one volume of his plays described them as agreeable.

clue.text: Judge of Jean-Jacques

parts.note: a translation of the title of the late dialogues of the Genevan philosopher, in which he judges himself

explanation.surface: Someone sitting in judgment on a Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: The philosopher's late work is titled (in French) '... juge de Jean-Jacques': he is judge of himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques wrote dialogues titled as his surname judging Jean-Jacques, himself.

clue.text: Source of reflections by Carroll?

parts.note: Lewis Carroll's Through the ... is about a mirror, a literal giver of reflections

explanation.surface: Asking where Lewis Carroll got his thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflections' looks like musings, but a mirror gives reflections, and Carroll's Alice goes through one.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirror gives reflections, and Carroll's sequel is Through the Looking-Glass.

clue.text: One of the Hispaniola hands

parts.note: the Hispaniola is the ship in Treasure Island; its crew includes the coxswain whose surname is Hands

explanation.surface: A crew member of a Caribbean ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' is both crewmen and the coxswain's surname: the pirate coxswain in Stevenson's Treasure Island is called Israel Hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Israel Hands was a pirate crewman aboard the Hispaniola in Treasure Island, so one of its hands.

clue.text: All her pupils were the crème de la crème

definitions.text: All her pupils were the crème de la crème

parts.words: All her pupils were the crème de la crème
parts.note: Muriel Spark's schoolmistress, Miss Jean ..., tells her girls they are the crème de la crème

explanation.surface: A teacher's boast about her elite class.
explanation.walkthrough: In Muriel Spark's The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, the teacher tells her chosen girls they are the crème de la crème.
explanation.definitionFit: Muriel Spark's teacher called her favoured pupils the crème de la crème.

clue.text: Source of lyrics by Chatwin?

parts.note: Bruce Chatwin's The Songlines is about the Aboriginal song paths, so their country is where the 'lyrics' come from

explanation.surface: Asking where the travel writer found his song words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lyrics' suggests a songwriter, but Chatwin's The Songlines traces the Aboriginal songs mapping that continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Chatwin's The Songlines describes the Aboriginal song paths across this continent, the land the songs come from.

clue.text: Household shoot was thus unrefined

definitions.meaning: Geoffrey Household wrote the thriller A ... Shoot, so his shoot was described by this word

explanation.surface: A domestic shooting party turns out to be crude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Household' looks like domestic, but it is Geoffrey Household, English thriller writer of A Rough Shoot (1951).
explanation.definitionFit: Household's novel is titled A Rough Shoot, and rough also means coarse or crude.

clue.text: "He's the only person I know who enjoys genuine-satisfaction" (Ayckbourn)

definitions.text: "He's the only person I know who enjoys genuine-satisfaction" (Ayckbourn)

parts.words: "He's the only person I know who enjoys genuine-satisfaction" (Ayckbourn)
parts.note: a line from Alan Ayckbourn with a gap for the kind of person who takes pleasure in failing

explanation.surface: A quotation from an Ayckbourn play about a man's strange pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed quotation has lost its gap: the line describes someone who enjoys genuine satisfaction from always coming off worst.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who habitually fails is the one who is always beaten, yet he relishes it.

clue.text: Lawrence's chanting choristers were seen in one of cypresses

definitions.text: Lawrence's chanting choristers were seen in one of cypresses

parts.words: Lawrence's chanting choristers were seen in one of cypresses
parts.note: D. H. Lawrence's poem 'Cypresses' pictures a line of the trees as chanting choristers along a road

explanation.surface: A poet watching a choir among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: In D. H. Lawrence's poem 'Cypresses', the trees lining a road are likened to choristers; a road lined with trees is this.
explanation.definitionFit: A broad road lined with trees on either side, like the cypresses in Lawrence's poem.

clue.text: A norm of conduct for William Trevor

definitions.text: A norm of conduct for William Trevor

parts.words: A norm of conduct for William Trevor
parts.note: William Trevor's first novel was A ... of Behaviour, and a norm of conduct is such a benchmark

explanation.surface: A rule of behaviour set by a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: William Trevor's first novel (1958) is A Standard of Behaviour; 'norm of conduct' paraphrases that title.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is a benchmark or yardstick, and William Trevor's first novel is titled A Standard of Behaviour.

clue.text: Zola's Vérité a novel example of one

definitions.text: Zola's Vérité a novel example of one

parts.words: Zola's Vérité a novel example of one
parts.note: Zola's novel Vérité belongs to his cycle Les Quatre Évangiles, and its title translates as a single fact that holds

explanation.surface: A remark on Zola's novel being an example of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Vérité is French for the abstract quality, so the novel is literally one example of the plural answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Vérité means verity, so the novel's title is one of the plural facts named by the answer.

clue.text: Will die like a —— - —— rebel. Don't waste any time in mourning organize." (Joe Hill)

definitions.text: Will die like a —— - —— rebel. Don't waste any time in mourning organize." (Joe Hill)

parts.words: Will die like a —— - —— rebel. Don't waste any time in mourning organize." (Joe Hill)
parts.note: the labour activist Joe Hill's last message before his execution, with the hyphenated adjective for a loyal rebel left blank

explanation.surface: A condemned union man's last words urging comrades to organize.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Hill, the Wobbly songwriter executed in Utah in 1915, wrote 'I will die like a true-blue rebel'.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyphenated adjective means staunchly loyal, steadfast to the cause.
